Upon the grace manifested to Israel "in the wilderness" God grounds His argument for renewing His favors to them now in their exile; because His covenant is "everlasting" (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.3">Jr 31:3</reference>), and changes not. The same argument occurs in <reference osisRef="Hos.13.5">Ho 13:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.9.10">9, 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.14.4">14:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.5.8">5, 8</reference>. Israel gratefully acknowledges in reply God's past grace; but at the same time tacitly implies by the expression "of old," that God does not appear to her now. "God appeared to me of old, but now I am forsaken!" God replies, Nay, I love thee with the same love now as of old. My love was not a momentary impulse, but from "everlasting" in My counsels, and to "everlasting" in its continuance; hence originated the covenant whereby I gratuitously adopted thee (Mal 1:2; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.28">Ro 11:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.29">29</reference>). Margin translates, "from afar," which does not answer so well as "of old," to "in the wilderness" (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.2">Jr 31:2</reference>), which refers to the olden times of Israel's history.<div eID="gen18287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18288" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with loving kindness ... drawn--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hos.11.4">Ho 11:4</reference>). Rather, "I have drawn out continually My loving kindness toward thee." So <reference osisRef="Ps.36.10">Psa 36:10</reference>, "Continue (Margin, 'Draw out at length') Thy loving kindness." By virtue of My everlasting love I will still extend My loving kindness to thee. So <reference osisRef="Isa.44.21">Is 44:21</reference>, "O Israel, thou shalt not be forgotten of Me." <div eID="gen18288" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv10257"/><div sID="gen18297" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv10257"/>7. The people are urged with praises and prayers to supplicate for their universal restoration. Jehovah is represented in the context (<reference osisRef="Jer.31.1">Jr 31:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.8">8</reference>), as promising immediately to restore Israel. They therefore praise God for the restoration, being as certain of it as if it were actually accomplished; and at the same time pray for it, as prayer was a means to the desired end. Prayer does not move God to grant our wishes, but when God has determined to grant our wishes, He puts it into our hearts to pray for the thing desired. Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.102.13-Ps.102.17">Psa 102:13-17</reference>, as to the connection of Israel's restoration with the prayers of His people (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.1-Isa.62.6">Is 62:1-6</reference>).<div eID="gen18297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18298" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for Jacob--</hi>on account of Jacob; on account of his approaching deliverance by Jehovah.<div eID="gen18298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18299" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">among--</hi>"for," that is, on account of, would more exactly suit the parallelism to "for Jacob."<div eID="gen18299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18300" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chief of the nations--</hi>Israel: as the parallelism to "Jacob" proves (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.19.5">Ex 19:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.135.4">Psa 135:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.6.1">Am 6:1</reference>). God estimates the greatness of nations not by man's standard of material resources, but by His electing favor. <div eID="gen18300" type="x-p"/>

Ramah--</hi>In Benjamin, east of the great northern road, two hours' <hi type="bold">journey from Jerusalem. Rachel, who all her life had pined for children (<reference osisRef="Gen.30.1">Ge 30:1</reference>), and who died with "sorrow" in giving birth to Benjamin (<reference osisRef="Gen.35.18">Ge 35:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.35.19">19</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.2">1Sa 10:2</reference>), and was buried at Ramah, near Beth-lehem, is represented as raising her head from the tomb, and as breaking forth into "weeping" at seeing the whole land depopulated of her sons, the Ephraimites. Ramah was the place where Nebuzara-dan collected all the Jews in chains, previous to their removal to Babylon (<reference osisRef="Jer.40.1">Jr 40:1</reference>). God therefore consoles her with the promise of their restoration. <reference osisRef="Matt.2.17">Mt 2:17</reference>, 18 quotes this as fulfilled in the massacre of the innocents under Herod. "A lesser and a greater event, of different times, may answer to the single sense of one passage of Scripture, until the prophecy is exhausted" [Bengel]. Besides the temporary reference to the exiles in Babylon, the Holy Spirit foreshadowed ultimately Messiah's exile in Egypt, and the desolation caused in the neighborhood of Rachel's tomb by Herod's massacre of the children, whose mothers had "sons of sorrow" (Ben-oni), just as Rachel had. The return of Messiah (the representative of Israel) from Egypt, and the future restoration of Israel, both the literal and the spiritual (including the innocents), at the Lord's second advent, are antitypical of the restoration of Israel from Babylon, which is the ground of consolation held out here by Jeremiah. The clause, "They were not," that is, were dead (<reference osisRef="Gen.42.13">Ge 42:13</reference>), does not apply so strictly to the exiles in Babylon as it does to the history of Messiah and His people--</hi>past, present, and future. So the words, "There is hope in thine end," are to be fulfilled ultimately, when Rachel shall meet her murdered children at the resurrection, at the same time that literal Israel is to be restored.
